Can you sketch 2–3 committed reservation options (cluster size, minimum GPUs, suggested ramp schedule) and an example failure/fallback policy if we hit urgent spikes? Procurement is already asking for a rough term sheet and standard SLA language.

Alex — thanks for the numbers, this is helpful. Quick summary below, then a more detailed playbook attached.

Option A — Conservative (Entry)
- Cluster: 8 x A100-equivalent GPUs
- Min guaranteed GPUs: 8
- Typical throughput: supports ~50 concurrent requests at p95 300–350ms for our baseline model; good for pilots and light production traffic
- Ramp: immediate activation (2 weeks) with 2-week warm-up and review at month 1

Option B — Performance (Recommended)
- Cluster: 24 x A100-equivalent GPUs (3 racks)
- Min guaranteed GPUs: 20 (buffer for maintenance/evacuation)
- Typical throughput: ~180–220 concurrent requests at p95 < 350ms given 600-token avg; supports primary model + reranker in-line
- Ramp: 4-week activation with staged warm pool (10% burst reserve) and monthly scaling review for 3 months

Option C — Headroom (Committed Growth)
- Cluster: 48 x A100-equivalent GPUs
- Min guaranteed GPUs: 40
- Typical throughput: >400 concurrent requests; designed for aggressive growth and multi-region failover
- Ramp: 8–12 week phased activation with test cutovers and canary routing

Fallback / surge policy suggestion:
- Primary routing to committed cluster (min GPUs). If queue latency breaches p95 target > 400ms for 3 consecutive minutes, auto-fallback to burst pool in shared hosted tier with rate-limited capacity and degraded p95 target (600–800ms). For critical customers we can configure token-level routing to prefer cached prefixes and shorter context models.

I've attached a short playbook that maps your CSV into likely GPU footprints and the sample term sheet. Hannah — can you add recommended SLA exceptions and notes on billing cadence?

Ben

Alex — adding operational and contractual detail. A few highlights to help procurement and your cloud team plan: 

- Activation windows: we define "activation" as when GPU instances are assigned and warmup starts. Conservative option can be activated in ~14 days; larger clusters require an orchestration and hardware alignment period (4–8 weeks).
- Min GPU guarantee vs. hot-burst: commitments lock a minimum quantity for billing and isolation; hot-burst capacity is available as best-effort and billed at a premium on consumption. We recommend keeping a 10–20% hot-burst allowance for expected spikes.
- Warm cache / KV behavior: during ramp we'll pre-load common prefixes where you have repeat traffic. That reduces observed p95 by ~15–25% and can materially lower GPU needs during peak windows.
- Graceful degradation policy: for spikes beyond hot-burst we will perform prioritized routing: A) cached responses, B) lightweight distilled model, C) shared-hosted fallback. We document the expected degraded latency for each tier.

Procurement notes: 
- Billing: monthly in arrears for committed capacity + metered hot-burst. Upfront credits available for annual agreements.
- Term sheet: standard 12/24-month commitment options; SLA includes uptime and p95 latency targets for committed cluster when running above 80% of min GPUs.

Next steps: Ben to produce a one-page term sheet for procurement. Karthik, can you surface an acceleration/activation checklist (networking, peering, certs) we should include in the onboarding timeline? Alex — when's good for a 30m review this week?

Thanks,

Alex, procurement — attaching a short onboarding checklist and a proposed 3-phase ramp schedule we typically use for mid-sized customers (I included timelines mapped to your volume estimates):

Phase 0: Pre-provisioning (1 week)
- Exchange network details, verify VPC peering, agree on KMS/HSM key fingerprinting; share account-level CIDR whitelist.

Phase 1: Pilot activation (2–4 weeks)
- Provision 8–24 GPUs depending on option chosen, enable KV prefix caching, run load tests with your payload, baseline latency and token costs.

Phase 2: Scale to committed minimum (4–8 weeks)
- Add remaining GPUs to reach min guaranteed; activate autoscaling policies and hot-burst lanes; run a canary cutover for traffic routing.

Operational safeguards: multi-zone placement for GPUs, automated evacuation windows, and a warmup script to pre-initialize model KV caches. For Nimbus numbers, my recommendation: start with Option B (24 GPUs, min 20) and commit to a 3-month review that could convert to Option C if growth materializes.
